property_summary: For any caller who is owner and any contract balance, calling withdrawAll always empties the contract balance (address(c).balance == 0) in the reference; the mutant that uses transfer to msg.sender can fail to transfer when the recipient's receive/fallback reverts, leaving a nonzero contract balance.

For any recipient contract with a fallback that reverts, the correct contract C (which uses a low-level call in sendMoney) ensures withdrawAll (which calls withdraw -> transfer) behavior differs: specifically, when sendMoney previously allowed controlled low-level calls, the general rule we test is that calling withdrawAll as owner always leaves address(c).balance == 0 in the reference but the mutant can leave a non-zero balance when the recipient's transfer reverts; the test uses a reverting recipient to make the mutant fail while the reference succeeds.

For any owner caller and any funded contract balance, calling withdrawAll always results in address(c).balance == 0 (reference) whereas the mutant using transfer to msg.sender can leave a nonzero contract balance if sending to a recipient whose fallback/receive reverts.

For any owner and any contract balance, calling withdrawAll on the reference C always empties the contract (address(c).balance == 0) because it calls withdraw which uses transfer to send to msg.sender; the mutant that replaces withdrawAll with a direct transfer can fail (leaving a nonzero balance) when the owner is a contract whose receive/fallback reverts, so the rule is violated for some adversarial owner contract.

For every owner address and any contract balance, calling withdrawAll as the owner always succeeds (does not revert) on the reference C, but the mutant that replaces the internal withdraw(...) call with a direct transfer to msg.sender can revert when the owner is a contract whose receive/fallback reverts, so the mutant fails for some adversarial owner contract.

Only the owner can withdraw the contract balance: for every caller and deposit amount, the reference contract preserves that after a call to withdrawAll only the owner can reduce contract balance (non-owner cannot withdraw), whereas the mutant missing the onlyOwner check allows some non-owner caller to drain funds.

For every caller and deposited amount, only the owner can cause withdrawAll to succeed in transferring the contract balance out (i.e., non-owner calls to withdrawAll must not change address(c).balance); the mutant removes the onlyOwner check so some non-owner call can reduce address(c).balance.

For all callers and deposit amounts, only the contract owner can successfully withdraw the contract's balance via withdrawAll (non-owners cannot change address(c).balance by calling withdrawAll); the mutant removing onlyOwner allows some non-owner call to reduce address(c).balance.

For every external caller that is NOT the owner and for any deposited amount, calling withdrawAll MUST revert (because onlyOwner enforces owner-only execution); the mutant removes that check so there exist non-owner callers and deposit amounts for which withdrawAll succeeds and thus the property is violated.

For any caller A and any deposit amount, if A is not the owner then calling withdrawAll must NOT transfer Ether to A (address(c).balance must remain unchanged for non-owners); the mutant (which removes the onlyOwner guard) allows some non-owner to decrease address(c).balance by calling withdrawAll.

For any caller who is the owner and any positive contract balance, calling withdrawAll transfers the contract's entire balance to the owner (reference); the mutant that calls withdraw(1) instead breaks this by leaving most of the balance in the contract for some fuzzed balances.

For any initial contract balance and owner caller, calling withdrawAll transfers the entire contract balance to the owner (so address(c).balance becomes 0); the mutant that calls withdraw(1) instead leaves a nonzero balance for some inputs, violating this rule.

For any positive contract balance and when the owner calls withdrawAll, the reference contract sends the entire contract balance to the owner (so address(c).balance == 0 afterwards); the mutant that calls withdraw(1) leaves a nonzero balance for some balances, violating this rule.

For any caller who is the owner and any contract balance B, calling withdrawAll causes the contract to transfer exactly B to the owner (so address(c).balance == 0 afterwards); the mutant that calls withdraw(1) instead can leave a nonzero contract balance for some fuzzed balances, violating this rule.

For any starting contract balance and when the owner calls withdrawAll, the reference contract empties the contract (address(c).balance == 0) after the call; the mutant that always withdraws 1 wei can leave a non-zero balance for many starting balances, so the property (balance becomes 0) is violated by the mutant for some fuzzed balances.

For any caller address and any contract-deployed intermediary, the original contract allows the designated owner (owner == address that deployed C) to successfully withdraw the contract balance via withdrawAll; the mutant that checks tx.origin == owner can block owner when the call is relayed through a contract (tx.origin != msg.sender), so there exist inputs (a relay contract caller) that make withdrawAll fail under the mutant but succeed under the reference.

If the deployer (owner) calls withdrawAll directly or through an EOA, the call always succeeds on the correct contract; the mutant that requires tx.origin == owner can be broken by calling withdrawAll through an intermediate contract (so withdrawAll can revert when relayed), therefore the property: "whenever the owner (deployer) invokes withdrawAll directly (msg.sender == owner), the call succeeds" holds for the reference but is violated by the mutant when the owner is not tx.origin (i.e., call comes from a contract).

For any caller address and any target callee, when the contract owner (deployer) initiates a withdrawAll (possibly by using an EOA as msg.sender) the reference contract always allows the withdrawal to succeed when msg.sender == owner, but the mutant that checks tx.origin == owner can be made to fail when the owner call is relayed through an intermediate contract (so withdrawAll may revert); the test fuzzes an arbitrary withdraw amount and uses a deployed relay contract to distinguish the two behaviors.

The correct contract allows the deployer (owner) to successfully call withdrawAll whether they call directly or are the immediate msg.sender (require checks msg.sender==owner); the mutant that uses tx.origin==owner can be made to revert when the deployer’s call is relayed through an intermediate contract (tx.origin!=msg.sender), so there exists a relay caller that breaks withdrawal.

The deployed owner (deployer) can always successfully call withdrawAll (call completes) when they are the immediate msg.sender; the mutant that checks tx.origin==owner instead of msg.sender can be made to revert when the owner’s intent is routed through a contract, breaking this universal property for some inputs (a contract caller).

For any caller who is owner and for any withdrawal amount not exceeding the contract balance, the reference contract always reduces the contract balance by that amount (i.e. forwards the ETH to owner); the mutant that replaces transfer with an unchecked low-level call can fail to send ETH and thus leave the contract balance unchanged for some inputs (fuzzer will find an amount and adversarial recipient behavior that causes the call to fail).

For any caller that is the owner and any withdrawal amount, the reference contract always transfers the requested ETH out (so address(c).balance decreases by that amount), but the mutant using an unchecked call can fail to forward ETH to a malicious/failing recipient causing address(c).balance to NOT decrease for some inputs.

For any caller and amount, in the correct contract only the owner can successfully withdraw funds (non-owners cannot increase address(c).balance change or receive funds), whereas the mutant allows non-owners to execute withdraw and thus change balances for some inputs.

For any target and amount, the reference contract's sendMoney does not revert when the callee's fallback reverts (because it uses low-level call which returns false but does not revert the caller), whereas replacing call with transfer makes sendMoney revert for some targets/amounts (callee revert), so the reference always returns ok=true while the mutant can return ok=false for some inputs.

For any target that rejects/consumes funds (i.e., whose fallback reverts), the reference contract's sendMoney call (which uses low-level call) will revert when the external transfer fails, whereas the mutant using send() will not revert and thus leave a different observable outcome; therefore, for all amounts and actor setups the reference will revert when sending to a reverting recipient, but the mutant will sometimes succeed (not revert) — breaking the rule.

For any target address whose fallback/receive always reverts, the reference C's sendMoney(...) (which uses low-level call and bubbles up callee reverts) will always cause the call to revert (so an external call to c.sendMoney reverts), whereas the mutant using payable(...).send(...) will not revert and will return false, so there exists inputs (an amount > 0) where the mutant does not revert while the reference does — detect this by asserting that try/catch shows the call reverted (ok == false) for all admissible inputs.

For any target address whose receive/fallback always reverts and any positive value, the reference C's sendMoney(...) call always reverts (bubbling the callee revert), whereas the mutant using payable(...).send(...) will NOT revert (it returns false), so there exist fuzzed inputs (a positive value and the reverting helper address) where the mutant does not revert but the reference does.

For any target that accepts or rejects funds, calling sendMoney on the reference C always propagates (reverts) when the callee's fallback reverts for any positive amount, whereas the mutant using .send(...) does not revert on such failing transfers; the test asserts that calling sendMoney to a reverting helper with a positive amount always reverts on the reference contract.

For any target address whose fallback consumes gas but does not revert, calling sendMoney with a positive value always forwards all gas and thus the reference's low-level .call will allow the callee to execute its fallback (so the call does not revert and the callee's side-effects occur); replacing .call with .send (which limits gas and returns false on failure) can prevent the callee from receiving enough gas to run its fallback and thus can change whether the call succeeds — the test asserts that when calling sendMoney towards a helper that emits an event in its fallback, the reference always results in the callee's fallback being executed (observable by measuring address(c).balance change due to the helper forwarding funds back), while the mutant can fail to execute the fallback for some fuzzed amounts.

For any sendMoney call that succeeds (does not revert), the reference contract C never changes depositsCount (it remains the same before and after); the mutant increments depositsCount during sendMoney, so for some inputs (a successful send to a payable contract) depositsCount differs after the call.

For any successful external call target, invoking sendMoney does not change depositsCount in the reference implementation (it only changes when fallback/receive on C is invoked), whereas the mutant increments depositsCount inside sendMoney so depositsCount after a successful send can be greater than before.

For any target contract and amount, calling sendMoney does not change C.depositsCount in the correct contract (it only changes when C itself receives funds via its fallback/receive), whereas the mutant increments depositsCount inside sendMoney so depositsCount can increase after sendMoney for some target/amount combinations.

For any caller and any target/value, only the contract owner can cause C to transfer out Ether via sendMoney (so address(c).balance never decreases when a non-owner calls sendMoney); the mutant removing onlyOwner allows a non-owner to make the contract send Ether and thus can decrease address(c).balance for some inputs.

For any caller and any amount, in the correct contract only the owner can make the contract send Ether out (so address(c).balance does not decrease when a non-owner calls sendMoney); the mutant that removes onlyOwner allows a non-owner to make the contract send Ether, so there exist caller/amount inputs that decrease address(c).balance.

For any caller and any target/value, in the correct contract only the owner can make the contract send Ether out via sendMoney, so address(c).balance never decreases when a non-owner calls sendMoney; the mutant removing the require allows some non-owner/callee combinations to decrease address(c).balance (e.g., when the callee accepts Ether), violating this rule.
